review_note: Align slides and notes with the lecture: keep the protocol jokes and scripts, remove assigned student reactions, and make decoding examples provisional. Preserve all slide boundaries and exercise timings.

edits.before:
If you've answered with a day and a time and watched the other face do something complicated, you know.

If you've never once wondered, you know too --- and you couldn't say how.
edits.after:
Answer with a day and a time, and the other person's face may do something complicated.

The line can be an invitation or a way to say you'd like to stay on friendly terms.
edits.reason: Keep the awkward coffee example without assuming the audience's knowledge or ability to explain it.

edits.before: - Both halves of the room have the same information here and only one of them can state it. That asymmetry is the week.
edits.after: - Ask what would help distinguish an invitation from a friendly sign-off.
edits.reason: Replace a scripted claim about the room with a question that exposes the ambiguity.

edits.before: - Ask the room for the payload before you reveal it. Someone will get it, and someone won't, and that's the week.
edits.after: - Ask the room for possible payloads before revealing this one.
edits.reason: Do not predict success and failure or treat the worked interpretation as the only possible answer.

edits.before:
An envelope marks a place where the sender didn't know the answer.

<MarginNote label="Diagnostic">Find the uncertainty and you've found the payload.</MarginNote>
edits.after:
A hint can protect the sender from a refusal --- or leave an understood request off the record.

<MarginNote label="Diagnostic">Ask what can be declined or left unsaid.</MarginNote>
edits.reason: Keep both strategic-speaker cases visible: a hint can manage uncertainty or avoid putting a mutually understood request on the record.

edits.before: - This is the week's most portable line. Stop asking "why are they being like this" and ask what they are not sure of.
edits.after: - Ask what the sender is unsure of, or what either person can decline or leave off the record.
edits.reason: Keep the diagnostic questions without ranking the line, inventing the audience's complaint or treating uncertainty as the only reason for a hint.

edits.before: A hint you both understood perfectly is still **not a thing either of you said**.
edits.after: The **request itself remains unsaid**, even when both of you understood it.
edits.reason: Align with the lecture's distinction between the spoken hint and the request left off the record.

edits.before: **Two minutes.** Compare with the pair beside you. Disagreements mark lines doing two jobs.
edits.after: **Two minutes.** Compare with the pair beside you. Write down both possible payloads where you disagree.
edits.reason: Align the activity with the lecture and leave disagreement open to investigation.

edits.before: - Everything up to here could be taught as instructions for the person who missed it. This is the slide that stops that.
edits.after: - Ask what the result requires of the sender when a hint is missed.
edits.reason: Replace commentary on the slide's moral purpose with the practical question it supports.

edits.before: - This is week 2's curse of expertise arriving at the level of one sentence.
edits.after: - Compare this sender-side error with week 2's discussion of expertise; keep the two experiments distinct.
edits.reason: Preserve the cross-week comparison without presenting the findings as the same mechanism.

edits.before: **If you send envelopes:** your estimate of how clear that was is biased in a measured direction, and knowing it doesn't make you a good judge. Send the second one plainer.
edits.after: **If you send envelopes:** check what the listener understood. If needed, send the second one plainer.
edits.reason: Match the lecture's usable instruction and remove the untested claim about knowing the result.

edits.before: **If you miss them:** a missed hint is a two-sided event with a documented sender-side error in it.
edits.after: **If you miss them:** the sender may have overestimated how clear they were.
edits.reason: Do not turn the experimental tendency into a guaranteed explanation of every missed hint.

edits.before: - But notice which way the surprise ran, and that they printed it. That is a functioning specification process, and it is why the result is worth more than the expectation before it.
edits.after: - Distinguish the authors' prediction from their reported result.
edits.reason: Keep the factual distinction without turning it into praise of a functioning specification process.

edits.before: - Some will find the bare version unsendable. That reaction is data, and week 6 gives it a price.
edits.after: - If the bare version feels unsendable, have students record why and keep the note for week 6.
edits.reason: Allow the response to emerge from the exercise rather than forecasting it.

edits.before: - Under this protocol, they will. That's the reassuring half: the sender retries.
edits.after: - Offer the rule as a limit on decoding effort, not a guarantee that the sender will retry.
edits.reason: Remove reassurance that depends on an unsupported prediction of someone else's behaviour.

edits.before: 3. **Payload:** Tuesday is bad, and they don't want to be the one who blocks it.
edits.after: 3. **Possible payload:** Tuesday is bad, and they don't want to be the one who blocks it.
edits.reason: Keep the worked example while marking an inferred intention as provisional, consistent with the over-decoding section.

edits.before: - Step 2 is the one they skip. Assuming co-operation is what makes the inference possible at all -- that is Grice's whole move.
edits.after: - Pause at step 2: the worked interpretation assumes co-operation. Ask whether the face-value reading also works.
edits.reason: Replace an invented student omission with a check on the example's assumption.

edits.before: - The third part is the one that does the work. Without it the question reads as a test of their sincerity.
edits.after: - Point out the practical reason for asking: whether to put a meeting in the calendar.
edits.reason: Keep the script's concrete purpose without guaranteeing how the listener would read a shorter version.

edits.before: The cost is **asymmetric**. An hour of your thinking; nothing of theirs. Which is exactly why nobody tells you you're doing it.
edits.after: You may spend time decoding a hint the speaker never meant to send. They may have no reason to notice.
edits.reason: Replace invented costs and certainty about others' awareness with the same possible failure mode.

edits.before: - If they needed more, they will send a second envelope. Under this protocol, they reliably do.
edits.after: - Leave room for the sender to clarify; do not promise that they will.
edits.reason: Match the lecture's removal of the unsupported reliable-retry claim.

edits.before: - If the face-value reading works and nothing was expected, that is the over-decode -- an hour of your thinking and nothing of theirs, which is why it goes unnoticed.
edits.after: - If the face-value reading works and nothing was expected, ask how much time went into decoding it and whether the other person had any reason to notice.
edits.reason: Align the audit with the lecture's open observations rather than supplying a cost and explanation in advance.

edits.before: Plus: an envelope marks the sender's uncertainty, and the sender is a biased judge of its clarity.
edits.after: Plus: an envelope can manage uncertainty or leave a request off the record. Senders can overestimate how clear they were.
edits.reason: Align the recap with the higher-order-deniability case and the bounded sender-bias result.
